title: DLMF 25.11 Hurwitz Zeta Function: The function \zeta\left(s,a\right) was introduced in Hurwitz ( 1882 ) and defined by the series expansion
summary: DLMF 25.11 Hurwitz Zeta Function: The function \zeta\left(s,a\right) was introduced in Hurwitz ( 1882 ) and defined by the series expansion
body: NIST DLMF section 25.11 (Hurwitz Zeta Function) says: "The function \zeta\left(s,a\right) was introduced in Hurwitz ( 1882 ) and defined by the series expansion \zeta\left(s,a\right) has a meromorphic continuation in the s -plane, its only singularity in \mathbb{C} being a simple pole at s=1 with residue 1 . As a function of a , with s ( \neq 1 ) fixed, \zeta\left(s,a\right) is analytic in the half-plane \Re a>0 . The Riemann zeta function is a special case: For most purposes it suffices to restrict 0<\Re a\leq 1 because of the following straightforward consequences of ( 25.11.1 ): Most references treat real a with 0<a\leq 1 . For \widetilde{B}_{n}\left(x\right) see § 24.2(iii) . When a=\frac{1}{2} , ( 25.11.10 ) reduces to ( 25.8.3 ); compare ( 25.11.11 ). For other series expansions similar to ( 25.11.10 ) see Coffey ( 2008 ) . In ( 25.11.18 )–( 25.11.24 ) primes on \zeta denote derivatives with respect to s . Similarly in §§ 25.11(viii) and 25.11(xii) ." Equation 25.11.1 on the page has alt text "\zeta\left(s,a\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(n+a)^{s}},". Equation 25.11.2 on the page has alt text "\zeta\left(s,1\right)=\zeta\left(s\right).". This card records that section's wording and equation alt text. It does not retypeset a formula the alt text did not carry.
